measurement.happened:
The single dominant story of the week in Saudi Arabia was a sustained and escalating campaign of Houthi missile and drone attacks on the kingdom's cities, airports, and oil infrastructure. Between October 17 and 24, the Houthis struck or targeted King Fahd International Airport in Dammam (killing at least two people), Riyadh airport (which was forced to restrict traffic), an Aramco oil field in the Eastern Region (killing two more), and the Dhahran headquarters area. A tanker was hit by an unknown projectile off the Saudi coast, and a Saudi helicopter crashed near the Yemen border killing two troops. The Saudi-led coalition intercepted multiple waves of ballistic missiles and drones, but the volume and accuracy of the strikes clearly exceeded what the air-defense network could comfortably absorb. The Wall Street Journal headline 'Saudi Arabia's Military Limitations Are Being Exposed by Houthi Attacks' captures the mood: the kingdom that spent decades building a layered air-defense shield found itself taking repeated hits on high-value targets. (Supporting headlines: Reuters Oct 24, 22, 20; AP Oct 21, 22; BBC Oct 22; Bloomberg Oct 21, 22; Al Jazeera Oct 22; TV5Monde Oct 22; DW Oct 18; FT Oct 18; CNBC Oct 18.)

In direct response, Saudi Arabia's international partners moved quickly to shore up its defenses. The United Kingdom announced it would deploy Typhoon fighter jets to conduct defensive air missions over Saudi territory, a significant step that Al Jazeera framed as part of a long British-Saudi military bond stretching back to World War I. Egypt's President Sisi went before parliament on October 17 seeking authorization to provide military support to Saudi Arabia if asked, and the Egyptian Security Council agreed to back the kingdom, though the formal parliamentary vote was delayed to October 26. Turkey submitted the Mecca defense pact (a trilateral agreement with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan) to its own parliament for ratification. France's President Macron made a surprise 'solidarity' visit to Riyadh and secured extra diesel supplies. The United States ordered some embassy staff and their families to leave Saudi Arabia, a move that is rarely used unless the State Department expects a further deterioration. (Supporting headlines: Reuters Oct 20, 21; AP Oct 20, 21; BBC Oct 20, 21; DW Oct 21; Al Jazeera Oct 20, 21; CNBC Oct 20; FT Oct 20; Bloomberg Oct 20, 21; CNN Oct 20, 21.)

The economic fallout was immediate and visible. Brent crude topped $110 for the first time in five months, and oil futures logged their biggest weekly gain in weeks. Saudi Aramco ordered its Dhahran headquarters staff to evacuate and work remotely, and the CEO publicly said the company was seeking partnerships with other countries to expand its overseas oil stockpile as a hedge against further disruption. The kingdom postponed its flagship Future Investment Initiative (FII) summit, the so-called 'Davos in the Desert,' from late October to 2027, and also pushed back a UN data forum. The Japan Football Association's chief said hosting the Asian Cup as scheduled was 'not easy' given the security situation. Thousands of Indian pilgrims were stranded in Saudi Arabia as flights were cancelled. Private jet charter costs out of the kingdom soared. The IMF warned that Saudi Arabia and the UAE were heading for recession amid the Iran-war impact. Gulf stock markets fell on multiple days. Yet Saudi crude exports in August hit a five-month high, and Aramco's expansion of its missile-plant production was reported, suggesting the kingdom is trying to project strength on the supply side even as its own infrastructure is under fire. (Supporting headlines: Reuters Oct 22, 23; Bloomberg Oct 22, 23; CNBC Oct 20, 23; WSJ Oct 22; FT Oct 20; DW Oct 23; Al Jazeera Oct 23; BBC Oct 23; AP Oct 21.)

A second, smaller but persistent thread was the OpenAI bugging scandal. A former OpenAI employee, a Saudi-linked engineer, was accused by US prosecutors of planting a surveillance device in a conference room and of having Saudi royal backing. A US judge ordered him held in detention without bail, calling him a 'precious talent' for Riyadh. The case is still in its early legal stages but it added a layer of diplomatic awkwardness and raised questions about Saudi intelligence reach into Silicon Valley. (Supporting headlines: Reuters Oct 19; AP Oct 19; BBC Oct 19; Bloomberg Oct 19; WSJ Oct 19; FT Oct 19; CNBC Oct 19; Al Jazeera Oct 19; TV5Monde Oct 19.)

Diplomatically, Iran offered to mediate between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis, but both sides reportedly did not answer. The GCC issued a joint condemnation of the Houthi attacks. Bangladesh pressed Saudi Arabia for an explanation after two Bangladeshi nationals were executed without prior notification. Egypt called for renewed Yemen talks. The US was reported to be reading possible strikes on Iran after its midterms, adding a background risk. Saudi Arabia's King Salman chaired a cabinet meeting in Riyadh, a signal of normal governance under pressure. The Saudi Pro League continued its match schedule, with multiple fixtures played on October 18, 19, 20, 21, and 24, a small but telling sign that daily life and even entertainment were being maintained. (Supporting headlines: Reuters Oct 21, 22; Al Jazeera Oct 18, 19; Bloomberg Oct 22; BBC Oct 20, 24; DW Oct 19; CNBC Oct 22.)
measurement.expected:
Theme 1 – Continued Houthi strikes and Saudi air-defense engagements. Confidence: almost certain. The Houthis have been firing at a high tempo for a week and show no sign of pausing, especially with Iran reportedly still backing them and no ceasefire in sight. Expect at least one or two more missile or drone waves aimed at airports, oil terminals, or the Eastern Province in the next seven days. The Saudi coalition will intercept most but some will get through, and there will likely be at least one more fatality or minor infrastructure hit. The Houthis will claim successes; Saudi Arabia will claim the vast majority were shot down. The cycle of attack-and-intercept is now the baseline rhythm of the conflict.

Theme 2 – Egypt's parliamentary vote on October 26. Confidence: almost certain that the vote takes place on or very near that date. Sisi has already framed it as 'necessary support' and the Security Council has agreed. The delay was procedural, not political. Expect a large majority in favor, probably with some opposition MPs abstaining. The practical effect may be modest in the short term (Egypt is not sending ground troops into Yemen, as Sisi explicitly ruled out), but the political signal to the Houthis and to the Gulf will be significant. Egypt may dispatch a naval escort, a few fighter jets, or a logistics package rather than a full expeditionary force.

Theme 3 – UK jets operational over Saudi airspace. Confidence: probable. The deployment was announced on October 20 and the Typhoons are likely already in the region or en route. Expect the first active defensive patrols within the next few days, possibly including intercepting or shadowing Houthi drones. There is a small risk of a close encounter or a misidentification incident, but a full UK-Saudi air battle remains unlikely. The UK will frame every mission as 'defensive.'

Theme 4 – Turkey ratifying the Mecca defense pact. Confidence: probable. The bill is already in the Turkish parliament. The ruling party has signaled support. Ratification could come within the next ten days, though Turkish parliamentary calendars can be unpredictable. Once ratified, the trilateral Saudi-Pakistan-Turkey framework becomes a formal treaty, giving Saudi Arabia a stronger legal basis to call on allied forces. Pakistan's role is likely to remain more symbolic (troops guarding Mecca) than operational against the Houthis.

Theme 5 – Oil prices and Aramco operations. Confidence: almost certain that Brent stays above $100 and likely in the $105-$115 range for the week. Aramco will continue to manage its Dhahran staff remotely or in reduced capacity. The CEO's push for overseas storage partnerships will generate more headlines as specific countries (India, Japan, South Korea) are named. Saudi crude exports will remain elevated as buyers scramble to lock in supply before the next escalation. The IMF recession warning for the Gulf will be cited in every major financial briefing.

Theme 6 – Saudi diplomatic outreach and the 'safe-haven' question. Confidence: probable that the BBC's 'safe-haven reputation' narrative gains more traction. Expect MBS or the foreign minister to make a public statement reaffirming that Saudi Arabia remains open for business and that the kingdom's sovereign credit and investment pipeline are intact. The postponement of FII will be framed as a precaution, not a retreat. Macron's visit will generate a follow-up statement on France-Saudi energy cooperation. The US will continue to walk a fine line between supporting Saudi defense and not wanting to be seen as fully committed to a Yemen war.

Theme 7 – The OpenAI bugging case. Confidence: possible that there is a procedural development (a bail hearing, a first court appearance, or a media leak from the Saudi side). A full-blown diplomatic row is possible but not yet certain. The case will keep generating headlines in tech and defense press but is unlikely to dominate the Saudi news cycle compared to the Houthi war.

Theme 8 – Asian Cup and sports. Confidence: possible that the hosting question gets more formal. The Japan FA chief's comment will be followed by a joint statement or a private meeting between the Saudi and Japanese football federations. The Saudi Pro League will continue, but expect a few more matches to be played behind closed doors or with reduced attendance in the Eastern Region. The Dakar Rally moving to Africa in 2027 will be confirmed in an official press release.

Theme 9 – Economic and social life. Confidence: probable that the stranded-pilgrim and flight-disruption stories continue, especially for Indian and other South Asian visitors. Private jet and airfare costs will stay high. The IMF recession warning will be debated in Saudi policy circles, but the kingdom's fiscal position (large reserves, low debt) means a full-blown economic crisis is not imminent. The Saudi bourse will remain volatile, tracking oil and the Houthi headline cycle.

Less likely surprises (possible but I would not count on them):
- A Saudi retaliatory strike on a Houthi target inside Yemen (airstrike on a missile launcher site or a logistics hub). This has been building in the headlines ('Saudi Arabia vows response') and could happen on short notice. I rate this as possible, maybe 25-30 percent.
- A US or UK F-35 or Typhoon being hit by a Houthi surface-to-air missile, creating a small but dramatic incident. Unlikely but not zero.
- A sudden Iranian statement pulling the Houthis back or, conversely, a direct Iranian missile at a Saudi port. The US 'reading Iran strikes after midterms' headline adds a wildcard.
- A second OpenAI-related leak or a Saudi royal naming the engineer publicly, turning a legal case into a diplomatic spat.

Things I would NOT bet on in the next seven days:
- A full Saudi ground invasion of Yemen or a large-scale air campaign over Sanaa. The kingdom is in a defensive, not offensive, posture, and the partners are providing air cover, not ground support.
- A ceasefire or a formal mediation deal with the Houthis before the Egyptian vote lands. The Houthis have not answered Iran's mediation offer, and they are in a strong position right now.
- A Saudi succession crisis or King Salman stepping aside. He chaired a cabinet meeting on October 20 and the monarchy is under external pressure, not internal.
- A crash in oil below $95. The supply-risk premium is too fresh and Aramco is still exporting at high volumes.
- A major Saudi domestic protest or public unrest. The kingdom manages information well and the population is focused on the external threat.
- A second major terrorist or insider attack in Riyadh or Jeddah. The OpenAI case is a bugging scandal, not an active plot, as far as we know.
- The FII summit being rescheduled to a date in the next two weeks. It was pushed to 2027, and that is final for now.
emoji_reasons: The week was defined by repeated Houthi missile and drone strikes on Saudi airports, oil fields, and cities, with multiple interceptions and at least four confirmed fatalities, making bombing the single most consequential event.

The defining diplomatic-military response was a rapid coalition of external air-defense support from the UK, Egypt, Turkey, France, and the US, turning Saudi Arabia's defense into a multilateral operation.

The economic backbone of the story was oil: Aramco evacuations, Brent above $110, postponed investment summits, stranded pilgrims, and an IMF recession warning all trace back to the kingdom's petroleum sector under fire.

delta.motion: The dominant thread between the two photographs is the Houthi campaign, and it grew in both volume and geographic spread. The first photograph showed the Aramco headquarters hit and Riyadh airport shut, with debris falling on residential areas. The second photograph adds the King Fahd International Airport in Dammam struck (two killed), an Aramco oil field in the Eastern Region hit (two more killed), and the Dhahran headquarters area targeted. The Saudi-led coalition is still intercepting missiles and drones, but the Wall Street Journal's framing of Saudi military limitations being exposed signals that the kingdom's layered air-defense shield is being stretched past comfortable margins. A Saudi helicopter crashed near the Yemen border, killing two troops, adding a ground-level loss that was not present in the first week. The tanker hit off the coast from the first week is echoed by continued Red Sea tension, but the new casualties at Dammam and the oil field mark a clear step up in lethality. The international military response grew dramatically. In the first photograph, Egypt was seeking parliamentary authorization and Iraq was offering reassurances. In the second, the United Kingdom has committed Typhoon jets to defensive missions over Saudi territory, the United States has ordered some embassy staff and families to leave (a rare and serious signal), Turkey has submitted the trilateral Mecca defense pact with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan to its own parliament for ratification, and French President Macron made a surprise solidarity visit to Riyadh. The external defense umbrella went from a single regional neighbor (Egypt) to a multi-national coalition of Western and regional powers within seven days. The economic thread also expanded. The first photograph showed oil prices rising and Aramco offering extra spot cargoes. The second shows Brent crude topping 110 dollars for the first time in five months, the flagship Future Investment Initiative summit postponed not merely to remote attendance but a full year to 2027, Aramco's CEO publicly seeking overseas oil stockpile partnerships as a hedge, the IMF warning that Saudi Arabia and the UAE are heading for recession, and thousands of Indian pilgrims stranded with soaring private-jet charter costs. The OpenAI bugging case shrank from a front-page international story to a smaller, persistent legal thread: the suspect is held without bail, a judge called him a precious talent for Riyadh, and the case is in early stages, but it no longer dominates the news cycle. Sports and events shrank in prominence: the Pro League continued its schedule with matches played across the week, the Asian Cup is still uncertain (the Japanese Football Association called hosting it not easy), and the specific events from the first week (Six Kings Slam, FIFAe, BMX qualifier, golf) faded from the headlines. The Iran-Saudi diplomatic thread changed shape: instead of the expected back-and-forth of Saudi accusations and Iranian denials, Iran actually offered to mediate between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis, and both sides reportedly did not answer. A new thread appeared in the form of Bangladesh pressing Saudi Arabia after two Bangladeshi nationals were executed without prior notification, and the United States being reported as timing possible strikes on Iran to after its midterms, adding a domestic-political clock to the regional calculus. The AI-generated misinformation videos, the specific Cristiano Ronaldo match postponement, and the mother-of-all-bombs discussion from the first week vanished from the second photograph's headlines. The public-serenity motif from the first week (residents hearing windows vibrate but appearing calm) gave way to more visible disruption: evacuations of Aramco staff, stranded pilgrims, and a cabinet meeting chaired by King Salman as a signal of normal governance under pressure.
delta.wind: The expectation of more Houthi strikes and Saudi interceptions was marked almost certain, and it came true and then some. The Houthis hit new targets in Dammam, the Eastern Region oil field, and Dhahran, and the WSJ headline about Saudi military limitations being exposed went beyond the predicted pattern of more debris and more interception statements. The expectation was that the volume might not increase dramatically but precision would improve; in practice both volume and lethality increased, with confirmed deaths at two new sites. The expectation of Egyptian and regional diplomatic moves was marked probable, and it came true in a broader and faster form than predicted. Egypt's parliamentary vote was delayed to October 26, so the formal authorization did not land this week, but the UK Typhoon deployment, the US embassy evacuation order, the Turkish Mecca pact ratification, and the French Macron visit were none of them in the expectation. The prediction had named Egypt as the main external actor and mentioned emergency phone calls; reality produced a multi-national defense coalition and a physical military deployment within seven days. This is the biggest miss in the expectation: the international response was faster, broader, and more structurally significant (a trilateral defense pact going to parliament) than the forecast anticipated. The expectation of Iran-Saudi diplomatic posturing was marked probable, and it came true in a different form. The prediction was for Saudi statements blaming Iran and Iranian counter-denials. Instead, Iran offered to mediate, which is a more conciliatory and unexpected move, and both sides ignored the offer. The US midterms timing for possible strikes on Iran was not in the original expectation at all; the first photograph mentioned the mother-of-all-bombs under consideration, and the second photograph reframes it as a post-midterms decision, adding a domestic-political dimension that the expectation did not capture. The expectation of elevated oil prices and continued Aramco spot cargoes was marked probable, and it came true and exceeded. Brent topping 110 dollars, the IMF recession warning, the FII summit postponed a full year, and the Aramco CEO seeking overseas stockpile partnerships all went beyond the prediction of prices remaining elevated and Aramco reassuring buyers. The expectation of sports and events decisions was marked probable, and it came true in a muted form. The Asian Cup remains uncertain, the FII was postponed, and the Pro League continued, all as predicted, but the specific events from the first week faded and the JFA's not easy comment is a softer signal than a formal postponement or cancellation. The expectation of MBS making a public statement or appearing on camera was marked probable, and it came true in a different form. King Salman, not MBS, chaired the cabinet meeting, and the Aramco CEO's public statements and the IMF's fiscal-buffer reassurance carried the resilience message rather than a single crown-prince address. The expectation of the OpenAI case generating further coverage was marked possible, and it came true in a smaller form. The suspect was held without bail, the judge's precious talent remark added color, but the case did not escalate into a major diplomatic crisis or a US congressional hearing as the expectation had floated. Among the things the expectation said it would not bet on, none of the major items materialized: no full-scale Saudi air campaign, no direct Saudi-Iranian clash, no cabinet reshuffle, no sudden ceasefire, no Ras Tanura production disruption, no US strike on Iran yet, and no Asian Cup cancellation. The less-likely surprises were mostly avoided: no Houthi strike on the Ras Tanura export terminal specifically (an oil field was hit instead), no Egyptian ground-troop deployment (the vote is delayed), no Red Sea closure, no OpenAI settlement, and no major cyberattack. The overall pattern of misses points to a consistent underestimation of how quickly and broadly the international community would mobilize around Saudi Arabia's defense, and an overestimation of how bilateral and contained the Saudi-Houthi dynamic would remain. The expectation treated the situation as primarily a Saudi-Yemeni problem with Egypt as the main external variable. Reality showed it becoming a multi-polar security event with Western powers physically deploying assets, a trilateral defense pact moving through legislatures, and the US using embassy-evacuation signals. The economic impact was also underestimated: the expectation saw elevated prices and Aramco reassurance cargoes; reality produced a 110-dollar barrel, a recession warning, a year-long summit postponement, and a structural shift in Aramco's hedging strategy. The expectation was directionally sound on the Houthi escalation but structurally too narrow on the international response and too soft on the economic consequences.
delta.driver: The single force pushing Saudi Arabia from the first photograph to the second is the Houthi campaign's demonstrated ability to penetrate a heavily invested air-defense network and hit high-value economic targets with increasing accuracy, which in turn triggers a cascade of international military, economic, and diplomatic responses that compound the kingdom's exposure. Iran's intelligence and targeting support, as reported by the Wall Street Journal, gives the Houthis a force multiplier that turns a proxy war into a test of Saudi Arabia's strategic credibility. Every new strike on an airport or an oil field is not just a local incident but a global market event, because Saudi crude, the Red Sea shipping lane, and the kingdom's Vision 2030 investment pipeline are all priced into the world economy. The international community's rapid mobilization of Typhoons, embassy evacuations, a trilateral defense pact, and a French presidential visit is driven less by love of Saudi Arabia than by the need to protect their own oil imports, shipping routes, and alliance architectures. The underlying structural question that no one has answered yet is whether Saudi Arabia can sustain its transformation into a diversified, event-hosting, investment-magnet economy while its physical infrastructure is under sustained missile and drone attack, and the answers from this week (Brent at 110, FII pushed to 2027, IMF recession warning, Aramco seeking overseas hedges) suggest the cost of that question is rising faster than the kingdom's air-defense budget can absorb.

crystal.reasoning:
Starting from the present: Saudi Arabia is in the middle of its most sustained external military pressure in years. Houthi missiles and drones have hit Dammam airport, an Aramco oil field, the Dhahran headquarters area, and a tanker, with confirmed deaths at multiple sites. The air-defense shield that was the kingdom's signature achievement is being stretched past comfortable margins, and the Wall Street Journal's framing of 'military limitations exposed' marks a shift in how the world reads Saudi security. The international response has accelerated dramatically: UK Typhoons are deploying, the US has ordered partial embassy evacuation, France's Macron made a surprise visit, Turkey is ratifying the Mecca defense pact, and Egypt's parliamentary vote is scheduled for October 26, which falls squarely inside the forecast window. Economically, Brent is above 110 dollars, the IMF has warned of recession, the FII summit is pushed a full year, and Aramco is publicly seeking overseas stockpile hedges. The OpenAI bugging case has narrowed to a legal thread. Iran's mediation offer was ignored by both sides. The US is timing possible strikes on Iran to after its midterms, which in 2026 fall on November 3, just days after this forecast window closes.

Extending the motion: The Houthi campaign has been growing in volume, geographic spread, and lethality for two consecutive weeks. The natural extension is continued strikes, but the arrival of UK Typhoons and the operationalization of the multi-national defense umbrella change the interception math. The Houthis will likely test the new layer, possibly targeting a site they have not yet hit (Jeddah's King Abdulaziz Airport is the most obvious gap in their target list). The Egyptian vote on October 26 is a concrete, dated event that will either formalize a new tier of support or, if delayed again, signal domestic friction. The international coalition is moving from declarations to operations: Typhoons going from 'announced' to 'on station,' the Mecca pact moving from 'submitted to parliament' to 'voted on or further debated.' Economically, the 110-dollar barrel and recession warning create a new baseline; if strikes continue, the next threshold is 120, and OPEC+ will be forced to respond. The US midterms clock means Washington has a narrow window before November 3 to either act or signal inaction, and Saudi Arabia is caught in the middle of that calculus.

Correcting for the wind: Our biggest miss was treating this as a bilateral Saudi-Yemeni problem with Egypt as the main external variable. Reality produced a multi-polar security event with Western powers physically deploying assets and a trilateral defense pact moving through legislatures. We also underestimated the economic consequences: the expectation was elevated prices and Aramco reassurance cargoes; reality was a 110-dollar barrel, a recession warning, a year-long summit postponement, and a structural shift in hedging strategy. The lesson is to expect the next week to continue breaking the 'bilateral and contained' frame. The international response will not slow down; it will operationalize. The economic pain will not plateau; it will compound. The Houthi campaign will not pause because the world is watching; it will adapt to the new defense layer. I should also weight the less-likely surprises more heavily: a Houthi hit on Jeddah, a second tanker incident, or a Saudi formal request for US combat support are all more probable than they look given the momentum. What I would not bet on: a full Saudi air campaign, a direct Saudi-Iranian clash, a sudden ceasefire, a Ras Tanura terminal hit, a cabinet reshuffle, a US strike on Iran before midterms, a full Asian Cup cancellation, or the OpenAI case becoming a major diplomatic crisis. The motion says the situation is getting worse in a managed way, and the wind says we should expect the 'managed' part to be less managed than we think.

King Salman or MBS will make a public appearance or statement projecting stability, and the Pro League will continue its schedule. The Asian Cup will receive a formal status update, most likely a postponement of specific fixtures rather than a full cancellation. A less-likely but motion-supported surprise: a Houthi claim of shooting down or damaging a Saudi or allied aircraft, which would be a significant escalation in the narrative. Another: a Saudi formal, public request for US combat air support, moving beyond the embassy-evacuation signal into an explicit alliance invocation. What I would not bet on: a full Saudi air campaign against Yemen, a direct Saudi-Iranian military exchange, a sudden ceasefire, a hit on the Ras Tanura export terminal, a Saudi cabinet reshuffle, a US strike on Iran before November 3, a full Asian Cup cancellation, the OpenAI case triggering a US congressional hearing, or a formal Red Sea closure.

crystal.eli5:
Saudi Arabia is being hit again and again by missiles and drones from the Houthis in Yemen. Last week they hit airports and oil fields, and this week the pattern is likely to continue, maybe targeting a city they have not hit yet like Jeddah. The good news for Saudi Arabia is that a bunch of its friends are sending help: British fighter jets are flying in, Egypt is voting this week on whether to send more support, and France and the US are making big diplomatic moves. Think of it like a neighborhood where one house keeps getting rocks thrown at it, and now the whole block is setting up a security guard.

The money side is getting painful. Oil prices are really high because the world is worried that Saudi Arabia's oil infrastructure might get hit more. Big companies are looking for ways to store oil in other countries as a backup, and economists are warning that Saudi Arabia's economy could shrink. It's a bit like if your lemonade stand was the biggest one in town and someone kept throwing rocks at your pitcher, so everyone starts buying lemonade from other towns instead.

There's also a smaller story about a Saudi-linked engineer who allegedly planted a spy camera in a room at OpenAI, the company that makes ChatGPT. He's in jail in the US, and it's making Saudi and American diplomats a little awkward. It's not going to blow up into a huge crisis, but it's a persistent irritation, like a splinter you keep bumping into. And in the background, the US is waiting until after its own elections in early November to decide whether to do something about Iran, which is the country backing the Houthis. So everyone is watching the clock.
